newsitem.title: USA: French election raises EMU doubts in U.S..
newsitem.headline: French election raises EMU doubts in U.S..

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
The surprise weekend victory of a Socialist-led coalition in French elections has raised fresh questions among U.S. officials and analysts about Europe's plans to launch a single currency in 1999.

"I think it's much shakier now than it was," said one U.S. official, who declined to be identified. "I'm not predicting it's going to collapse, but the Socialist victory throws up a real question mark into what the French are going to do."

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, who was named prime minister on Monday, was swept into office by a disaffected French electorate that decisively rejected the austerity policies of President Jacques Chirac's government.

The Socialists have said they are committed to European economic and monetary union, but have also made clear they are unwilling to continue the tough budgetary policies conducted by Chirac to qualify for entry into the group.
They have also said they want Italy and Spain to be in the first wave of nations to adopt the single currency in 1999.
In a speech at George Washington University here Monday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Europe seemed to be going ahead with EMU -- at least for now.

"The European Union is a broad-based economic union which, at least for the moment, looks like it's heading toward EMU and a common central bank," he said, in response to a question comparing EMU with the North American Free Trade Agreement.

Speaking to reporters later, Rubin said he believed that European nations remain committed to monetary union, despite the French election and the battle in Gemany over a proposed revaluation of its gold holdings as part of entry into EMU.
"My impression is that the commitment (to EMU) remains intact," Rubin said.

The Treasury chief declined to specify the impact on the United States if EMU unravels, but said the whole issue of monetary union would be discussed at the economic summit of major industrial nations in Denver later this month.

Princeton University Professor Peter Kenen, a one-time adviser to the Treasury, said that he expects France to seek changes in the way EMU will operate after 1999, including alterations in Europe's so-called economic stability pact.
But he doubted that Jospin will try to end EMU outright. "He does not want to be the man who kills EMU," Kenen said.
Jospin's victory though will mean real headaches for German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, widely-seen as the driving force behind monetary union.

"The French electorate has grave reservations about European integration," said former Commerce Undersecretary Everett Ehrlich. "But it's not clear to me those translate into a dramatic slowing in progress toward a programme."

Ehrlich, who now heads consultants ESC Co. here, portrayed the economic policies espoused by Jospin as a step backward for France -- a view also held privately by some of his former Clinton administration colleagues.

The administration has made no secret of its belief that France and other European nations need to restructure their economies and do away with onerous labour market regulations to help bring down sky-high unemployment and promote growth.
The French Socialists have pledged to create 700,000 jobs for young people, but half of them would come in what some analysts here see as the already bloated public sector.
The Socialists have also promised to reduce the working week from 39 hours to 35 over five years without loss of pay, another step analysts here see as retrograde.
"The French election is something of a retreat from the future," Ehrlich said.

The United States has much at stake in a successful launch of EMU, analysts said. If monetary union goes ahead but is dramatically watered down by France, that could lead to a big surge in the dollar, making U.S. exports less competitive.

If EMU collapses completely into a bout of bickering throughout Europe, that could have implications for everything from the expansion of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation to the future of Bosnia.
"A disunited, fractionalized Europe is not good for global stability," said a U.S. official, who declined to be named.

"I've never felt that EMU is a threat to us," Rubin added. "I've always felt that the principal significance to us ... is the effect it's going to have on Europe. If it's good for Europe, it's good for us."
